passages.content: When gateway error rates climb, check whether the errors cluster on one endpoint or spread across all traffic. A narrow cluster usually traces to a single dependency; a broad rise across every endpoint points to something shared, such as a recent rollout or a saturated shared resource.

Cross-reference an error spike against the change log for the affected service first. A rollout that shipped in the same window is the fastest lead to check, before assuming the cause is load-related.

Elevated p95 latency without a matching error spike usually means requests still succeed but wait longer -- for a downstream call, a lock, or a busy connection pool. Check downstream timeout metrics before assuming the gateway itself slowed down.

A latency rise that tracks a downstream service's own timeout rate suggests the gateway is absorbing a slow dependency rather than being slow itself. Compare the two timeseries before narrowing further.

A burst of downstream timeouts followed by a growing retry rate can amplify itself: each timeout triggers a retry, which adds load to an already struggling dependency, which causes more timeouts. Check whether retry volume is rising faster than the underlying request volume.

If timeouts concentrate on one downstream service while the others stay healthy, the fix is scoped to that one dependency, not the gateway. Confirm which service is timing out before proposing a broader change.

A connection or worker pool running near its ceiling shows up as rising queue wait time well before requests start failing outright. Check pool utilization alongside latency, not error rate alone -- pressure often shows up as slowness first.

Pool pressure frequently follows a change that increased how long each request holds a slot -- a slower downstream call, a larger query, or a lock held longer than usual. Look for what changed in the request path before assuming raw traffic growth is the cause.

A configuration change landing right before a symptom starts is the highest-value lead to check first: line up the change timestamp against when the symptom timeseries actually turns, not just when the alert fired.
Not every change near an incident's start caused it -- confirm the change actually touched the affected service, or a service directly upstream of it, before treating the timing alone as proof.
